title: Father in Mississippi cotton country, then to uncle Vincent's grocery
summary: His father worked for an uncle in the Delta until the cotton crash, then for Vincent Matassa, a grocer and clarinetist in the Italian association band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Do you know this for a fact or did somebody tell you this?

Well, my father, yeah. And so he went to work for an uncle in a little town in Mississippi called Chula, T-C-H-U-L-A, Chula, Mississippi. It's in the Delta. It's in the Delta. Yeah, not far from Jackson and Greenwood and like that. It was cotton country. Oh, okay. Especially in those days. Right. And in fact, he was there through World War I until right after World War I and there was a cotton crash. In fact, there's a blues song that talks about 10 cent cotton and 30 cent meat. Right. Yeah. Okay. And that's what they're talking about, right? Okay, sure.

Okay, it's peaking too much. All right. In the red. And he came to New Orleans where he worked for another uncle. Mm-hmm. Which... That was Vincent Matassa who had a grocery store in the French Quarter and who was a clarinetist. He played in...
No, he was also... He was a clarinetist.

Yeah. He played in the Italian association band. Wow. You know, they'd march on Saints Day, feast days and church things and stuff like that. In fact, my father was particularly proud of that day that he was a soloist. Something about being a soloist meant something to him in those days. Mm-hmm.
The nearest thing to what today would call a marching band.
